query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy, the intrinsic chemical disorder and large atomic size mismatch generate a lattice with significant local distortions that, when thermally expanded between ~673 K and 1073 K, enhance the energy barrier for edge dislocation glide. This in turn counteracts the typical thermal softening, producing a yield‐strength plateau and unusual elastic response compared to conventional BCC alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, single‐phase, chemically disordered BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy with homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled tensile (or nanoindentation) tests while incrementally increasing the temperature from room temperature up to 1073 K; additionally, compare as‐cast samples with those receiving a thermal anneal designed to subtly promote short‐range order.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at constant strain rate, in an inert (e.g., Ar/H2) atmosphere to minimize oxidation; focus on the temperature range from ~673 K to 1073 K where anomalous stress retention is anticipated.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions arising from the large atomic size mismatch among Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr that modify the edge dislocation barrier energies when the lattice undergoes thermal expansion.
generation.mechanism: As the alloy is heated within the specified range, thermal expansion increases the lattice spacing nonuniformly due to pre‐existing distortions. This enhances the local energy barriers for edge dislocation movement (rather than reducing them as in conventional metals), thereby suppressing dislocation motion and maintaining a nearly constant yield strength despite rising temperatures. The degree of short‐range order may further modulate these local barriers.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under elevated temperature testing (673–1073 K), the yield strength and elastic moduli will show an anomalously weak temperature dependence (i.e. a plateau) relative to room temperature behavior, and samples with increased short‐range order (via annealing) will exhibit a more pronounced plateau or even higher yield retention. Additionally, diffraction measurements should reveal moderate, isotropic lattice strain changes despite the thermal expansion.
generation.baseline: Conventional BCC alloys (or the as‐cast state at RT) which typically exhibit a gradual decrease in yield strength with increasing temperature due to thermally activated dislocation glide.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in the temperature window roughly between 673 K and 1073 K; at temperatures significantly below this range standard elastic behavior dominates, and above this range other mechanisms (e.g. dynamic recovery or phase instability) may override the edge-dislocation barrier effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of edge dislocations relative to any residual screw dislocation activity and the influence of short-range ordering remain uncertain. The magnitude of yield strength retention may also vary with strain rate and minor compositional fluctuations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples: one as-cast and one annealed to promote slight short-range order. Perform a series of tensile or high-load nanoindentation tests at room temperature, then at controlled elevated temperatures between 673 K and 1073 K. Use in situ diffraction techniques (e.g., neutron or synchrotron XRD) and TEM to monitor lattice strain distributions and dislocation structures.
measurements: Yield strength and flow stress as a function of temperature
Elastic moduli and lattice strain (via diffraction techniques)
Dislocation density and character (via TEM) in samples tested at different temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (a) the yield strength and elastic moduli decrease monotonically with increasing temperature with no observable plateau in the 673–1073 K range; (b) the changes in dislocation structure do not correlate with a barrier effect (i.e. no evidence that edge dislocation motion is inhibited at elevated temperature); or (c) samples with enhanced short-range order do not exhibit a significantly different (or enhanced) strength retention compared to the as-cast samples.

cited_evidence.text: The plastic response of the Senkov HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy is explored by means of simulated nanoindentation tests. Both a random alloy and an alloy with chemical short-range order are investigated and compared to the well understood case of an elementary Ta crystal. Strong differences in the dislocation plasticity between the alloys and the elementary Ta crystal are found. The high-entropy alloys show only little relaxation of the indentation dislocation network after indenter retraction and only negligible dislocation emission into the sample interior. Short-range order—besides making the alloy both stiffer and harder—further increases the size of the plastic zone and the dislocation density there. These features are explained by the slow dislocation migration in these alloys. Also, the short-range-ordered alloy features no twinning plasticity in contrast to the random alloy, while elemental Ta exhibits twinning under high stress but detwins considerably under stress relief. The results are in good qualitative agreement with our current knowledge of plasticity in high-entropy alloys.

There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.
